title: Super funds scramble over safety of $6bn Nvidia investment
full_text:
Superannuation savings worth more than $6bn are caught up in Nvidia’s Chinese espionage scandal thanks to industry funds’ devotion to passive investing.
It’s prompted superannuation giant Hesta to put the chipmaker under close watch as pressure mounted on Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang.
Nvidia’s board – which had launched an independent investigation into the allegations – was reportedly preparing to oust Mr Huang, 63, following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset.
He has now resigned with Nvidia announing the decision on Thursday morning local time.
US House Republicans have ordered him to attend a closed-door hearing, escalating a rapidly unfolding succession and governance crisis at the US chipmaker.
Nvidia super
More than $US330bn was wiped off Nvidia’s market value earlier this week, testing the resolve of Australia’s biggest super funds which have more than $6bn in combined exposure.
Hesta, which owns about $888m worth of Nvidia shares, said it was “monitoring the issues that have surfaced this week”. Last year it placed WiseTech Global – another company engulfed in a governance crisis involving its founder – on its watch list.
It said it did not have further comment to make about Nvidia at this stage.
AustralianSuper, which holds about $1.46bn worth of Nvidia’s shares and sold its entire stake in WiseTech in March last year, declined to comment on Mr Huang’s crisis. The Australian Council of Superannuation Investors also declined to weigh in on the exposure of Australian retirement savings.
Other super funds with sizeable Nvidia stakes include UniSuper ($1.85bn), IFM Investors ($970m), Aware Super ($642m) and Cbus ($418m).
Writer and broadcaster Esther Krakue says NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang was taught an “expensive lesson” in what happens when you make stupid decisions.
The fallout threatens to reverberate across Nvidia’s local network of customers and strategic partners.
Among them is data-centre hopeful Firmus, which counts Nvidia as a major shareholder and partner, after the AI infrastructure player abandoned its $44bn float on the ASX due to a lack of support from local investors. Firmus declined to comment on how the crisis at Nvidia would affect its operations as it explores alternative capital-raising options.
Mr Huang founded Nvidia 30 years ago and has personally cultivated ties with governments and key customers worldwide. His departure will create a leadership vacuum at a critical juncture, threatening to slow the company’s breakneck execution.
Etoro lead analyst Josh Gilbert said the market “has only ever known Nvidia with Huang in charge; working out what it’s worth without him won’t happen overnight” and his departure would threaten to slow the AI build out.
“Jensen has built many of the relationships that underpin the AI boom, from Nvidia’s biggest customers to the Asian suppliers that build its chips, so his departure would be felt across the industry. Huang has been the brains behind the product and the chief salesman rolled into one, and finding both in one person is going to be a huge challenge,” Mr Gilbert said.
“Nvidia is central to the AI build-out and has also been one of its biggest funders, which raises questions about whether that support and the industry’s circular financing arrangements would continue without Jensen at the helm. None of this changes how many chips the big tech names want to buy, but investors want certainty at the top as much as they want growth. Right now, all they’ve got is uncertainty, and markets hate that.”
Market jitters have already surfaced in local trading platforms. Pepperstone’s 24-hour market recorded heavy selling as Australian retail investors rushed to manage risk ahead of Nvidia’s upcoming quarterly earnings.
Pepperstone head of research Chris Weston said that while a “bombshell” had hit Nvidia, it still provided “some of the best products on the market and that won’t change anytime soon”.
“But its ability to execute, sustain its competitive advantage and bring its pipeline of innovation to market is facing greater scrutiny, with investors questioning whether the same exceptional growth trajectory can be maintained under new leadership,” Mr Weston said.
“Nvidia isn’t simply facing the potential loss of a CEO. Investors are being asked to contemplate the possible departure of the individual who helped build the company’s competitive advantage, commercial relationships and strategic influence.”
After Jensen Huang: why the honeytrap is every boardroom's new problem
Mr Weston said Mr Huang’s departure would introduce execution risk across product development, customer commitments and the continued ramp-up of AI infrastructure.
“There’s also a geopolitical dimension. Nvidia is effectively a strategic asset in the US-China competition for AI leadership,” he said.
“Investors must assess whether heightened scrutiny could complicate Nvidia’s relationship with Washington or increase the risk of tighter export restrictions.
“When investors lose confidence in the assumptions underpinning a valuation, the share price becomes the mechanism through which that uncertainty is priced. And while uncertainty is always present in markets, when it clouds our ability to forecast future earnings with conviction and assign a fair value to those cash flows, volatility is almost invariably the result.”
Mr Huang has pledged complete co-operation with Nvidia’s investigation.
“I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” he said.
